place: Wadi Nuweiʿimeh (valley), NE of Jericho
landmark_required: a ruin: חריבה 'the (little) Ruin', taken as the place-name Ḥorebbeh ; steps (מעלות) 'that go to the east', in or attached to the ruin ; setting: the Valley of Achor (עמק עכור)
landmark_disputed: The ruin: ḥryb(ʾ)h 'little ruin' (Milik; Puech 2006 p.179) against ḥrwbh / ḥrwbhʾ (Lurie; Muchowski; Lefkovits p.31). The valley: עכור in Milik, Lefkovits and Puech; Pixner and García Martínez–Tigchelaar read עבור 'go past', which removes the valley. מעלות 'steps' is not disputed; the unit word that follows is (Puech אריח; Lefkovits אחת; Milik deletes it).
reason: Evidence: the published sources record ruins in the valley of several periods (Iron Age sites with building remains near Kh. el-Mefjer, Milik D4 p.263; a Christian village with a chapel, SWP p.226; Crusader–Mamluk sugar mills, Aronshtam p.99) and undated irrigation channels (Aronshtam p.91), but none reports steps or a ruin that can be named Ḥorebbeh. The ʿAujah aqueduct is now dated Hasmonean–Herodian (Aharonovich et al. 2025), against SWP's Crusader date (p.179). Inference: that the ʿAujah line crossed this valley rests on SWP p.179, which traces it to the ʿAin Duk / Nuweiʿimeh springs; and a ruin that was already old in the 1st century (such as the Iron Age sites) would suit a place called 'the Ruin', but no source links one to the entry. The identification stays at valley level.

No source reports a pair of cavities, tamarisks or buildings. Inference: on Puech's 'cavities' reading the kind of feature existed in the area in the right period, but the entry puts the pair 'in the valley', and nothing lets one choose a pair. The valley-level verdict (Onomasticon tradition) is unchanged.

place: Wadi el-ʿAṣla / Gofet el-ʿAṣla area, NW Dead Sea
landmark_required: an 'earth pit' (שית האדמא): a pit dug in ground, not rock (Puech 2015 p.52); Milik's 'Red Pit' in red marl (C15) ; position word שולי 'edge / bottom / outlet' of ʿAṣla; Milik takes it as a spring outlet (ʿEin Nebi Musa)

The IAA survey of the escarpment north of Qumran reports caves with Early Roman and 1st-century CE finds (Yitah et al. pp.180–185), but it does not name ʿAṣla. Inference: whether that survey area includes the ʿAṣla stretch cannot be settled from the report, and a cave is not the earth pit the entry needs. The marl terrain fits an 'earth/red pit' in kind only, so the 'possible' verdict stands on the modern name and the sequence.

place: Wadi Qumran below Kh. Qumran
landmark_required: a יגר in 'the valley (גי) of Sekakah': a cairn, tumulus or burial mound (Milik C77; Puech 2015 p.53) or, on Eshel's reading, a dam (CSS pp.101–102) ; setting: גי, a valley floor; Milik (C30) takes it to imply cultivated ground

reason: Evidence: both senses of יגר correspond to feature types published for Qumran in the settlement period: the dam at the head of the aqueduct (Eshel pp.94–95; accepted as existing by Puech p.53) and stone-capped graves (SWP p.210; Milik D8; Puech p.58). The IAA survey adds a tumulus and stone heaps at the foot of the escarpment beside the wadi, their date not established (Baruch et al. pp.197–198), and cliff caves with 1st-century use (pp.198, 212). Inference: the landmark type the entry needs existed in the area and period whichever meaning is chosen, but no report can single out 'the' cairn, and the verdict still depends on Sekakah = Qumran, not on archaeology.

place: Kh. Qumran (site, aqueduct, cisterns)

The required landmark, a conduit with a head, exists in the right period. Inference: 'the great stone' is restored and cannot be checked against any report. The Phase 3 verdict already rested on this aqueduct; the archaeology confirms the landmark but does not remove the dependence on Sekakah = Qumran, so the verdict is kept, not raised.

place: Kh. Qumran (site, aqueduct, cisterns)
landmark_required: a fissure (סדק), a natural crack (Milik C39; Puech 2015 p.55) ; reference landmark: אשוח שלומו, 'the reservoir / basin of Solomon', with the fissure to its east ; place: 'in Sokokah'

reason: Evidence: Kh. Qumran had a large reservoir and channel system in the settlement period (Milik 1960 p.147; Wexler p.viii; SWP p.210), and natural cracks and piping cavities in the surrounding marl are documented with 1st c. BCE–1st c. CE activity (Cohen and Porat 2020). Both landmark types therefore existed at the site in the period. No source attests the name 'Solomon's' for any reservoir, and Milik's own argument dates such a name after 68 CE (D11). Inference: the entry fits the site in kind; which basin, if any, bore the name is not established, so the site-level verdict is kept.

place: Wadi Kuteif

Inference: a tomb type is present in the wadi, but nothing shows a tomb there in the 1st century, and this output does not treat the reported chamber as the entry's tomb. The low, route-based verdict is unchanged.

place: Lower Jordan near Jericho (a ford; river level only)

Inference: a river crossing is a natural feature and was surely used in the period, but that is background, not a published finding; the cairn cannot be checked. The river-level verdict is kept.

place: Doq: Jebel Qarantal (Jebel Quruntul, Mount of Temptation)

Inference: on the 'fortress' reading the landmark type existed in the period; on Puech's 'drying room' no such installation is reported. The site-level verdict is kept at medium because the landmark word is disputed.

place: Wadi el-Qelt at Choziba (St George's monastery)
landmark_required: 'the mouth of the water outlet' (פי יציאת המים) at Koziba; Eshel: the head of an aqueduct ; הטור: a retaining wall (Milik C95, D20), parapet / mountain (Puech 2015 p.68), or הסור 'the rock' (Eshel p.105)

So 'water outlet' and 'retaining wall' match installations in use in the period. Inference: the landmark check succeeds, but the name Koziba is attested only from the 5th-century monastery, which is what limits the verdict; it stays best-supported, medium.

place: Tell es-Sultan (Old Jericho, Elisha's spring)
landmark_required: a mound or ruin-heap: 'the tell of Koḥlit' (תל); Eshel 'ruins' ; a conduit (אמא), with the opening at its northern edge ; an immersion installation a stated distance away: Puech's 'cold room (frigidarium) of the bath' (מקרת) or Milik's 'crevice of immersion' (ניקרת)

Inference: a ruin-mound suits Eshel's 'ruins of Kohlit', but the bath needed on Puech's reading is not found at the tell. The Koḥlit identification is still a hypothesis and stays 'possible'. landmark_required: gate: השער המזרחי 'the East Gate' (definite, no qualifier) ; cistern (בור) opposite the gate ; channel or conduit (מזקא) belonging to the cistern
landmark_disputed: The gate phrase is read the same way in all editions. מזקא 'channel' (Milik, Puech) against Allegro and Luria's במוקא. The distance figure differs between editions and is a feature of the text only. Thiering (CSS p. 285) takes 'the Eastern Gate' to be a courtyard door at Qumran; Phase 3 did not adopt this.
reason: Evidence: Warren's galleries in front of the Golden Gate met rock cuttings and walls that he does not date (Recovery pp. 153-158), and his survey lists many undated rock-cut cisterns with feed channels under the platform (pp. 204 ff.). The 1st-century east gate itself is known only from texts (Mishnah Middot, Neh 3:29; Lefkovits p. 127, Puech p. 184); BK: the standing Golden Gate is usually dated late Byzantine or Umayyad. Inference: cisterns with channels are common in the enclosure, so the landmark type is plausible, but no report dates such a cistern near the east gate to the 1st century, and the verdict stays where the texts put it.

place: Jerusalem, eastern wall/rampart (next to the East Gate of entry 9)
landmark_required: cistern (בור) under החומא 'the wall/rampart', on the east side ; rock projection or spur (שן הסלע) ; entrance under 'the great threshold' (הסף הגדול)
landmark_disputed: The landmark words are read the same way in all editions. בדין 'bars' (Puech) against כדין 'pitchers' (Lefkovits) concerns only the treasure. Lefkovits renders החומא 'city wall' (p.130), Puech 'rampart'. Whether the wall is the city's or the Temple enclosure's east wall is open. BK: in the 1st century the enclosure's east wall was also the city's east wall.
reason: Evidence: Warren describes rock scarps, deep debris and the masonry of the east wall and its south-east angle (Recovery pp. 135-141, 153-158), and undated cisterns with channels under the platform (pp. 204 ff.). No report read describes a cistern with a threshold under the east wall. Inference: rock outcrops and cisterns both occur along the east side at site level, so the landmark types fit, but nothing adds evidence of period, and the identification stays contextual (Puech p. 184; Lefkovits p. 130).

place: Valley of Shaveh / King's Valley near Jerusalem (Kidron–Hinnom area or el-Baqʿa; which valley is unresolved)
landmark_required: named area: השוא 'the Shaveh' (valley) ; fallow or unploughed land (שלף), the counterpart of the irrigated land of entry 37 ; a rock-cut underground chamber (צריח; Milik C80: a Roman-period tomb type) facing north
landmark_disputed: The toponym and שלף are read by all editions (Puech 2015 pp. 73-74). Lefkovits leaves שלף open as a possible toponym 'Shalef' (p. 265); Allegro read bšly. צריח is read by all the main editions.
reason: Evidence: rock-cut tombs of the Second Temple period are reported in the Kidron valley, including the three Akeldama tombs (Avni & Greenhut 1996, abstract; BK: near the Hinnom junction), and Clermont-Ganneau records a local 'valley of the king' name for the Kidron between the Haram and Bir Eyub (SWP III pp. 53-54). For el-Baqʿa the set has only Milik's statement that it was a necropolis (DJD III p. 274), with no report cited. Inference: underground tomb chambers of the period are common around Jerusalem, so the archaeology fits either candidate and cannot choose the valley; 'fallow land' cannot be tested, and the verdict stays low.

place: Valley of Shaveh / King's Valley near Jerusalem, its irrigated part (which valley is unresolved)
landmark_required: named area: השוא 'the Shaveh' ; irrigated land (רוי), which needs a water source nearby ; underground chamber (Puech, by emendation) or cippus/boundary stone (Milik)
landmark_disputed: Both landmark words are disputed. ברוי 'irrigated land' (Milik, Puech) against Lefkovits' בדין, a toponym 'Din' (pp. 268-269), and Beyer's bdwr. Puech's 'underground chamber' emends the engraved bṣwyh (2015 p. 74); Milik (and Puech earlier) read a cippus.
reason: Evidence: 19th-century descriptions put irrigated gardens below the Siloam pools, where the Tyropoeon, Hinnom and Kidron meet, and give that stretch of the Kidron a 'valley of the king' name (Wilson 1871 pp. 21-22; Clermont-Ganneau in SWP III pp. 53-54). No source dates the irrigation, and the set describes none at el-Baqʿa. Inference: only the Kidron–Hinnom candidate has a reported water source for an irrigated tract, which slightly favours it over Baqʿa, but the landmark word is disputed and the valley unfixed, so the verdict stays low.

place: Ramat Raḥel (Kh. Ṣaliḥ), Aharoni's Beth ha-Kerem
landmark_required: named place: Beth ha-Kerem (בית הכרם) ; a large built reservoir (אשוח/אשיח), not a household cistern (Milik C70) ; the reservoir has an entrance ('as you enter, on the left'), not a compass bearing
landmark_disputed: The toponym and the reservoir word are read the same way in all editions. Only the unit after 'to the left' differs (cubits: Puech, Lefkovits; 'feet': Milik; 'notches': Wolters). That is a feature of the text and does not bear on the site.
reason: Evidence: the excavators date the large plastered pools and channels at Ramat Raḥel to an earlier phase (probably late Iron Age), buried by a fill whose latest pottery is 2nd century BCE (2006-07 report, PDF pp. 16-18). In the Late Second Temple period the site was a small Jewish village with ritual baths and columbaria (INJ 17 pp. 59-60), with undated hewn cisterns on its slope and a probably Hasmonean aqueduct nearby (HA-ESI 137). Inference: the place was inhabited in the scroll's period, but no report describes a large reservoir in use then, and the pools Phase 3 knew only from BK were out of use; since Aharoni's identification partly rests on the scroll's own sequence (Lefkovits p. 333 n. 11), the entry can stay best-supported, but its confidence should fall from medium towards low.

place: Kidron valley at Absalom's monument, east/south-east of the city
landmark_required: named monument: יד אבשלום, the 'Hand' (monument) of Absalom (2 Sam 18:18: in the King's Valley) ; a free-standing monument with a west side (the side and depth are features of the text only)
landmark_disputed: The name is read the same way in all editions. Lefkovits notes that יד can mean 'place' (Targum 'the Place of Absalom') (pp. 348-349). Only the unit and verb in X 13 differ (Puech ḥpwr ʾmwt; Milik 'feet').
reason: Evidence: the standing Kidron monument is dated by style to the 1st century CE, and its earliest known labels (4th-century inscriptions) name Zacharias, not Absalom (Zias 2023). Josephus knew a marble stele of Absalom two stades from the city (Høgenhaven p. 79 n. 67), and Lefkovits reports that scholars do not equate today's monument with the biblical one (p. 348). Inference: a monumental funerary structure of the scroll's period stood in the Kidron, so type and date fit, but no source shows that it was called Absalom's in the 1st century; the Kidron placement still rests on sequence, and the verdict stays low.

place: Siloam, Jerusalem: Gihon outlet to the Siloam pool
landmark_required: named place: Siloam (שלוח) ; a water outlet or spring (Puech יציאת המים) or baths (Milik בית חמים) ; a trough or gutter (השקת) with the cache under it
landmark_disputed: The name depends on reading waw, not reš, and on Puech's restored של (2015 p. 92). Milik reads שלוחי 'of Siloah' qualifying 'the baths'. Lefkovits reads no place name ('of Jehu'); Lurie, Beyer and Wolters read 'of Rachel'. What kind of installation it is also differs: outlet or spring (Puech), baths (Milik), water closet (Lefkovits). השקת is read by all.
reason: [Corrected 2026-09-28 after the site review] The large stepped pool is Reich and Shukron's pool at Birkat el-Ḥamra; the HA-ESI street reports call it the Siloam Pool, but Szanton (ʿAtiqot 113, 2023, pp. 35, 38–42) identifies it as Solomon's Pool and the smaller Silwan Pool at the tunnel outlet as Siloam. The pool/outlet setting fits; a period trough of the required type is not established. Verdict: best-supported, medium, conditional on the Siloam reading (the high rating is withdrawn). Original reason follows: Evidence: IAA excavation reports describe, at Siloam, a monumental stepped pool used in the late Second Temple period, other stepped pools, water-supply systems and drainage channels, and a 1st-century CE street from the pool to the Temple Mount destroyed in 70 CE (Szanton 2024; HA-ESI 132, 134, 135). Wilson (1871 p. 22) records the pools fed from the Gihon through an underground channel. Inference: the landmark type, an outlet of water with pools and channels, existed and was in use when the scroll was written, which strengthens the Siloam placement; what remains is textual (waw against reš, and a restored של), which no report can settle.

place: Kidron slope below the south-east corner of the Temple enclosure (tomb of Zadok, not itself identified)
landmark_required: 'below the southern corner of the האסטאן': the stoa or portico (Milik, Puech: Solomon's Portico on the east side of the enclosure) ; named tomb: קבר צדוק, the tomb of Zadok ; tomb features: an exedra or vestibule (אכסדרן) with a pillar (עמוד)
landmark_disputed: האסטאן = 'stoa' (Milik D54; Puech 2015 p. 95) against Lefkovits' 'ossuary' (p. 366); under 'ossuary' the entry has no outside landmark. Pixner's ṣdyq 'the Just' needs an emendation. Exedra and pillar are read by all.
reason: Evidence: rock-cut tombs of the Second Temple period are reported in the Kidron (Avni & Greenhut 1996, abstract), and Milik puts the standing monumental tombs on the east bank (DJD III pp. 270-271). On the west slope, Warren's work at the south-east angle describes debris and masonry, not tombs (pp. 135-141), and the slope further south was a refuse dump in the 1st century CE (HA-ESI 136); BK: the east-bank tombs include a porch with columns, the kind of pillared vestibule the entry names. Inference: the tomb type fits the Kidron necropolis at site level, but the reported monumental tombs of this type stand on the east bank, which suits Jeremias's variant better than Milik's west-bank placement; the verdict holds at slope level, and the bank is left open.

place: Kidron valley, east slope opposite the (unlocated) tomb of Zadok
landmark_required: 'the top of the rock facing west' (ראש הסלע הצופא מערב) ; anchor: opposite the court or garden of Zadok (נגד גנת צדוק) ; a large slab (מסמא) at its base (not a site-level feature)
landmark_disputed: The two locating phrases are read by all editions. The first word is disputed: הכסח 'scarp' (Puech, Beyer), הבסה 'family plot' (Milik), תבסת 'ruin' (Lefkovits). So is the last phrase: Puech 'at its base, it is consecrated', Milik 'in its water channel'. Allegro's Siloam reading of XI 7 is a minority reading.
reason: Evidence: the Kidron's east side is a west-facing rock slope with rock-cut tombs and standing monuments of the Second Temple period (Milik DJD III pp. 270-271; Avni & Greenhut 1996; one monument dated by style to the 1st century CE, Zias 2023). Inference: a west-facing rock with tombs is well attested at site level in the right period, so the setting fits. But the entry is placed only relative to Zadok's court, which no source locates, so the verdict stays at slope level and low.

place: Pools of Bethesda (St Anne's), north of the Temple enclosure
landmark_required: a complex of two (or more) reservoirs: בית האשוחין 'house of the (two) reservoirs' (Puech, Lefkovits) or Milik's emended בית אשדתין 'Bet Eshdatain' ; a reservoir (אשוח/אשיח) in it ; its smallest basin, which one can enter (לימומית: Milik, Puech)
landmark_disputed: Only Milik's emended reading gives the name Bethesda. Puech (2015 p. 103) rejects it, but his own reading is a dual or plural 'reservoirs'. Lefkovits reads 'the basin, three cubits' (pp. 392-398); Allegro, Luria and Wolters read lw mymwt.
reason: Evidence: the editors report, from excavations they cite but which were not read for this phase (Vincent & Abel 1926; Jeremias 1949/1966), a double pool with a smaller northern basin at St Anne's, in use in the 1st century (John 5:2; Milik DJD III pp. 271-272; Høgenhaven p. 84). Warren describes a second rock-cut double pool nearby, at the Sisters of Sion (1871 pp. 196-197; BK: Josephus' Strouthion pool). Inference: feature and period fit St Anne's, but 'the house of the two reservoirs' alone does not single it out, because the same quarter had another twin pool; the identification still leans on Milik's emended name and the Eusebian tradition, so the verdict stays medium.

place: Jerusalem, the Herodian Temple enclosure (Temple Mount), as one block
landmark_required: 3: a great cistern in 'the court of the peristyle' (חצר הפרסטלון) ; 5: a spiral staircase or stairwell (המסבא) 'of Manos' ; 7: a cave of 'the old house of MDH/MRH' with a third platform or course (רובד) ; 8: an underground chamber (צריח) with a cistern, in 'the court of the wood stores' ; 12/12a: the southern and eastern corners of a court with a damaged, restored name (Milik: the peribolos) ; 13: a pit in the מלה (Milik, Puech: 'the Esplanade', the retaining walls and fill of the platform) ; 14: a tomb in or at the same מלה, on its east side
landmark_disputed: Most key words are disputed or restored. The court name in 12 is restored in every edition (Milik 'peribolos'; Puech δίαιτα '(?)'; Lefkovits נבט). In 13-14, מלה/מלח could be 'Esplanade' or 'Melaḥ'. In 8, בתי 'stores' is an emendation of engraved מתי. The key word of 7 is read המדה/המרה/המדח/חמדה. In 5, Puech's המסבא 'spiral staircase' ('graphically certain') replaces Milik's המעבא 'foundry'. Only 'peristyle' in 3 is secure.
reason: Evidence: excavation reports describe the Herodian enclosure's walls, corners and platform fill (Shukron & Reich 2011; Warren 1871 pp. 135-159) and undated rock-cut cisterns and underground chambers under the platform (Warren pp. 204 ff.). The peristyle court, the wood-store court, the spiral stair and a tomb by the esplanade are described only in texts (Josephus, Mishnah Middot, 11QTemple), as cited by Milik pp. 272-274, Puech pp. 182-184 and Høgenhaven pp. 56-58. Inference: the landmark types of 12/12a and 13 (corners, retaining walls, fill) and the cisterns and chambers of 3 and 8 fit the enclosure in site and period, but the inner-court and tomb landmarks cannot be checked archaeologically; since these entries fail on readings rather than on archaeology, they stay 'possible, low'.

place: Kidron gorge (Wadi en-Nar) near Deir Mar Saba
landmark_required: יגר: a heap of stones that may cover a burial, i.e. a cairn or burial mound (Milik DJD III C77 p.245; Puech 2015 pp.72-73; Høgenhaven p.74 'heap of stones') ; פי צוק הקדרון: 'the mouth / entrance of the gorge of the Kidron', a natural gorge (Milik DJD III D28 p.268; Puech 2015 p.73) ; on the Lurie/Eshel reading only: יגר = a dam at the head of an aqueduct (Eshel CSS pp.101-102)
landmark_disputed: יגר is read by all editions, but its sense is disputed: cairn/burial mound (Milik, Puech, Høgenhaven) or 'dam' (Lurie, Eshel), which Puech rejects (2015 p.73 n.298). צוק is 'gorge' for Milik and Puech, 'peak' for Lefkovits (p.262). The name is הקדרון (Allegro, Puech), הקדרוה (Milik; the same name) or הקדרות 'pottery' (Wolters, Pixner; Puech 2015 p.73 nn.299-300).
reason: Evidence: SWP III (pp.3, 219) shows Wadi en-Nar open near Jerusalem and a gorge by Mar Saba, so the named natural feature exists, but no source consulted records a cairn or burial mound there; Milik only infers that the scroll's cairns stood by paths (C77 p.245), which SWP's ancient road with wells down the valley (p.58) is consistent with but does not confirm. On the disputed 'dam' reading, Eshel (pp.95, 97, 102, from Patrich) describes a Herodian aqueduct head in the same stretch, so that reading does not move the site. Inference: Dahari (ʿAtiqot 41 pp.233, 239) shows the Kidron is also a canyon where it leaves the escarpment and was used in the 1st c. CE, so 'the mouth of the gorge' alone does not fix the Mar Saba end; that precision comes from Milik's and Puech's route reading, and Høgenhaven's up-valley route (p.74) would fit the lower end as well. The site-level verdict (the Kidron gorge) stays best-supported at medium; the landmark itself is unconfirmed and, as a heap of stones, could not be dated.

place: ʿAin en-Naṭuf, Wadi Khareitun (cave of St Chariton)
landmark_required: שובך: a dovecote (Puech 2015 pp.76-77; Høgenhaven p.75 n.54), a regular opening of a cave or rock face (Milik DJD III C4 p.238) or a tower (Lefkovits p.273); in every sense a built or rock-cut feature ; שולי/שולו הנטף: the base or edge of ha-Naṭoph; for Milik the point where the spring emerges (DJD III C5 p.239; D30 p.268) ; two holes or pits in the rock near it (Puech 2015 pp.77-78; Høgenhaven p.76 n.55): a detail of the text only
landmark_disputed: Only the landmark word: שובך = dovecote (Puech, Høgenhaven and most editors, Puech 2015 p.76 n.318), cave opening or inspection hole (Milik), tower (Lefkovits), drain (Schiffman, CSS p.191). The toponym הנטף is read by all editions; in šwly/šwlw the waws are engraved like reš (Puech CSS p.72).
reason: Evidence: SWP III (pp.357, 361, 375-376) and Milik (1960 p.150) confirm the spring, the cliff and large natural caves at the site, but the dated remains are late antique and medieval (Chariton's laura, 12th-century ruins), and no source consulted records a dovecote or a rock-cut opening at the spring. Milik (DJD III C4 pp.238-239) shows from texts that rock dovecotes were common and that the Herodium district bred pigeons for the Temple in the Roman period, while the excavated Herodian dovecotes that Puech cites (2015 p.77 n.318) lie elsewhere. Inference: the landmark type is plausible for the district in the period but is not attested at the site, so the identification still rests on the name alone; nothing here raises or lowers it.

place: Mount Gerizim (Jebel et-Tur) above Nablus
landmark_required: המעלה/המעלא: the step (or steps) (Milik DJD III p.274; Puech 2015 p.108; Lefkovits p.411) ; השית / השוח(ה) העליונא: 'the upper pit' or shaft; 'upper' implies at least one other pit (Lefkovits p.412)
landmark_disputed: The pit word is šyt (Milik and most editions) or šwḥ(h) (Puech 2015 p.108; Allegro šyḥ); the step is hmʿlh corrected to hmʿlʾ, and Allegro's 'entrance' is rejected by Puech. Neither changes the kind of feature: a pit or shaft with a step or steps.
reason: Evidence: SWP II (pp.187-190) and Bull's excavation as summarised by Lefkovits (p.412) describe steps, trenches and cisterns on the summit, so the kind of feature exists at site level, but every dated example is later: Hadrian's stairway (Milik p.274), the Byzantine church, fortress and reservoir (SWP II pp.189-190), and Bull's cisterns 'from a later period'. For 1st c. BCE-70 CE the sources consulted offer only texts: a Samaritan holy mountain with a tradition of hidden vessels (Josephus AJ 18.85, via Milik p.274 and Høgenhaven p.86). BK: Josephus (AJ 13.254-256) says John Hyrcanus destroyed the Samaritan temple in the late 2nd c. BCE; the modern excavation reports (Magen et al., Mount Gerizim Excavations, 2004 onward) were not accessible here, so a stepped pit of the period can be neither confirmed nor excluded. The name-based verdict stands.

place: Beth Shean / Scythopolis (Beisan), at a spring of the town
landmark_required: פי המבוע: 'the mouth of the spring', a flowing spring with a defined outlet (all editions); Milik (DJD III C2 p.238) takes it as the orifice of a monumental fountain from which the spring water flows
landmark_disputed: None for the landmark. The letters of the toponym are agreed; only its identification is disputed (Beth Shean with final mem, Beth Shem(esh), 'House of the Name', or an unknown Beth Shem: Puech 2015 p.109 and nn.488-491; Lefkovits p.414).
reason: Evidence: 19th-century descriptions stress that Beisan has several large perennial springs and streams, one named after the Roman theatre (SWP II pp.81, 102, 105, 107), and IAA reports describe 'numerous springs' and a dam and pool of the 1st c. BCE-1st c. CE that stored water in the city's farmland (Har'el 2016; Horowitz and Atrash 2016), with Early Roman burial at the town's edge (Tzin and Najar 2022). So a spring with an outlet is attested at site level and water was being managed in the period; the 'main fountain' that Milik has in mind is known only from 4th-12th-century writers (DJD III pp.261-262). Inference: feature fit improves from 'partial' to 'good', but springs are common in the Beth Shean valley and cannot tell candidates apart; the verdict still rests on reading בית שם as Beth Shean, which Greenfield disputes (Lefkovits p.414), so it stays best-supported at medium.

place: Kh. Ibziq (Bezek), north-east of Nablus
landmark_required: ביבא הגדולא: 'the great conduit', a large built drain or water channel at a settlement (Puech 2015 p.110 'large conduit'; Lefkovits 'large drain'; Høgenhaven p.85 'large pipe') ; בית הבזך / בית הכוך: 'the house of Bezek' or 'the burial chamber' near it (Puech 2015 p.111), a building or tomb
landmark_disputed: The landmark word ביבא is not disputed (Puech rejects bkwkʾ, 2015 p.111 n.501). The toponym is: hbzk (Allegro, Puech, Lefkovits), hbrk (Milik), hkwk (Wolters), hkrk (Beyer) or hbwr (Wilmot, Wise) (Puech 2015 p.110 nn.494-498); the second instance may be bzk or kwk.
reason: [Updated 2026-09-29 after the Phase 5 source follow-up] Zertal's Manasseh Hill Country Survey vol. 2 (2008) was read for the two Ibziq sites. Upper Kh. Ibziq (site 44, pp. 195-198): 45 cisterns, reused caves, a Roman road east of the site; no conduit, drain or channel; pottery LR 20%, Byz 30%, EM 10%, MA 30%, no Hel and no ER in the percentages, but two ER vessels illustrated (Fig. 122 nos. 8, 10). Lower Kh. Ibziq (site 42, pp. 191-193): about 70 burial caves, 45 cisterns; pottery Byz 80%, EM 20%. Zertal takes the sites as Eusebius's two Bezek villages but places biblical Bezek at Kh. Salhab (site 23, pp. 104-107, 151-153; ER 15%, no conduit). Verdict: possible, low. The conduit is still unreported, the period fit is weak, and Salhab may have had the name in the scroll's period. See phase5_source_followup.md. Original reason follows: Evidence: the only site description available (SWP II p.237) records undated traces of ruins, cisterns and caves at Kh. Ibzik; no source consulted describes a large conduit or drain there or dates any remains to the 1st c. BCE-70 CE, and Puech accepts the site only 'for lack of anything better' (2015 p.110). The modern survey of the Manasseh hill country (Zertal et al.) was not accessible here. Inference: the landmark and the period remain unchecked, so the verdict stays 'possible', resting on the Eusebian name evidence and on the contested bzk reading.

place: Hyrcania (Kh. el-Mird) and its aqueducts, as proposed by Eshel
landmark_required: 16: an אמא (conduit, aqueduct) 'going to [ ]', with a distance 'as you enter'; Eshel restores 'to Hyrcania' and takes it as Hyrcania's northern aqueduct (CSS pp.102-103) ; 29: an אמא 'of Q[...]' and 'the northern reservoir' (האשוח הצפוני) with four sides; Eshel restores Qi[dron] (or Cy[pros]) and takes the conduit as Hyrcania's southern aqueduct and the reservoir as one of its pools (CSS pp.103-105) ; 35: a יגר read as 'dam' at the head of Hyrcania's southern aqueduct in Wadi Qidron (Eshel CSS p.102, after Lurie)
landmark_disputed: Every link to Hyrcania rests on a restoration or a disputed meaning. 16: the lacuna after הבאה is restored [בר]כא 'pool' by Puech, left blank by Milik and Lefkovits, and 'Hyrcania' only by Eshel. 29: קי[ is restored qyb[wṣ] (Puech), qy[ṣyṣ] (Milik), Kypros or Kidron (Eshel); Puech judges the Kidron restoration too long for the space and Kypros 'ruled out' (2015 p.64 n.252), and Eshel notes that col. VIII spells קדרון without yod (p.105 n.31). 35: 'dam' for יגר is rejected by Puech (2015 p.73 n.298).
reason: Evidence: Eshel (pp.95, 97, summarising Patrich) and SWP III (p.212) describe at Hyrcania the kinds of feature these entries need (aqueducts, a dam at an aqueduct head, pools and cisterns), and Eshel dates the northern aqueduct as presumably Hasmonean and the southern one as Herodian, with the fortresses garrisoned in the 1st c. CE (p.92); Wexler's preface (ʿAtiqot 41 pp.vii, xii) lists the system among surviving Roman-period water works. So the landmark types were in place in the period. But the tie to the entries comes only from Eshel's restorations and his reading of יגר, which Puech rejects on space and sense (2015 pp.64, 73), and archaeology cannot decide what stood in the lacunae (inference). The block stays 'possible, low'.

place: Tekoa–Herodium sector (Puech's area for IX 4–X 4); area only, no site identified
landmark_required: 39: a (vine) terrace on Puech's reading, and an underground chamber or hypogeum (צריח) facing east ; 40: underground chambers (צריחי), probably burial chambers, natural or man-made (Høgenhaven p.76), with a channel or gutter (זרב) ; 41: a hole or pit (קומעה) (Puech 2015 pp.81-82) ; 42: a waterfall (קול המים) or a dam/reservoir (qyl), by the bend of a built water conduit (ביב) (Puech 2015 p.83) ; 43: a pit (שית) north of the mouth of a gorge (צוק) at Beth Tamar, in stony ground ; 44: a dovecote (שובך) in a 'small fort' (מצדנא), in a structure of at least two levels (Puech 2015 p.86) ; 45: a (re)plastered cistern (בור גר) of channels (מזקות) fed by 'the great wadi' (Puech 2015 p.87)
landmark_disputed: Several landmarks depend on the reading: 39 bḥblt 'terrace' (Puech) or the toponym Tekelet ha-Šani (Milik); 40 ḥwryn/drwm or ḥwrwn/ym; 41 qwmʿh 'hole' or Milik's emended Qobʿeh; 42 lkpt byb 'bend of a conduit' or Milik's Kephar Nebo; 44 šbmṣdnʾ 'small fort' or Milik's Masada with an aqueduct; 45 bbwr gr 'plastered cistern' or Milik's bkyrgr (wheel-well). שובך is dovecote or opening, as in entry 38.
reason: Evidence: 19th-century descriptions of the sector report a fortress, a large reservoir and an aqueduct at Herodium (SWP III pp.27, 330-331), which SWP ties to Herod through Josephus, plus rock-cut tombs, cemented cisterns and a spring at Tekoa, cultivated land by Tekoa, and natural caves and gorges in Wadi Khureitun (SWP III pp.296-300, 357-382); so most landmark types of entries 39-45 (fort, reservoir, cistern, conduit, tomb chambers, caves, gorge, terraced land) occur in the area. Only the Herodium works are placed in the 1st c. BCE by these sources; the rest are undated or later, dovecotes are attested for the district only in texts (Milik C4), and no 'Beth Tamar' or 'Maṣadona' is located. Inference: the types fit Puech's area but do not narrow it to any site; the relevant modern survey (Hirschfeld 1985) was not consulted, so the area-only verdict is kept.
